body: This was proven in human tissue in 1989 and it settled one argument.
punch: It also started a bigger one that still isn't resolved.

headline: The estrogen camp
body: Human genetics and clinical trials both point to estrogen as the dominant lever on growth plate closure and adult bone density.

headline: If it's all estrogen
body: Human osteoblasts carry functional androgen receptors — demonstrated directly in human cells, and later localised within human bone tissue.
punch: A receptor that exists is a receptor doing something.

headline: And DHT
body: DHT cannot be aromatised into estrogen. Yet DHT specifically upregulated androgen receptor levels in human bone cells and amplified their response — while estradiol did not.
punch: A non-convertible androgen produced an effect estrogen couldn't.

headline: Cartilage also converts
body: Both articular and growth plate cartilage metabolise testosterone into DHT on site, with DHT the dominant metabolite accumulating there.
punch: The machinery for direct androgen action is physically present.

headline: But then
body: Testosterone and the non-aromatisable androgen oxandrolone were tested in organ culture and had no effect on baseline longitudinal growth rate at all.

headline: And these two papers
body: Chagin cites the earlier work directly and argues the results aren't strictly contradictory — preventing suppression is a different claim from promoting growth.
punch: This is a real scientific disagreement, not a synthesis artefact.

headline: So the honest answer
body: Direct androgen action on bone cells is real and demonstrated. Whether it meaningfully drives longitudinal growth specifically is contested at the bench, not settled.
punch: Receptors existing doesn't tell you what they accomplish.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
